title: Rhodes from the other shore
subtitle: The conquest of 1522 and Ottoman Rhodes, told from Süleyman's side

chapters.title: Standing on the other shore
chapters.text:
Most visitors meet the siege of 1522 from inside the walls. They stand on the Street of the Knights, look up at the Palace of the Grand Master, walk the moat below the Tower of Spain, and hear how a few hundred knights held out for six months against an army of a hundred thousand before sailing away with their banners flying. It is a good story, and much of it is true. But its shape was set by the people who wrote it down first: knights, chaplains, a Venetian engineer, and the French and Italian chroniclers who had the news in print within a few years.
This piece tells the same events from the other shore. It begins in Istanbul, follows Sultan Süleyman's army down through Anatolia to the harbour at Marmaris, crosses the strait with it, and stays in the Ottoman camp until the Knights have gone and the Friday prayer is said in the town. It is a re-centring, not a reversal. Ottoman court writers had their own purposes. They wrote for a dynasty, a conquest was proof of God's favour, and they say little about doubt or about ordinary soldiers. Both archives need the same careful reading.
The Ottoman side has something the European side lacks: a day-by-day campaign diary kept by clerks travelling with the sultan's household. It covers 233 days, from the crossing of the Bosphorus on 16 June 1522 to the return to Istanbul on 29 January 1523. It survives inside the collection of state papers that Feridun Bey assembled in the 1570s, and a Turkish transcription was published in 2017. Most of the Ottoman detail below comes from it. The translations are mine, from the printed Turkish, and are paraphrase rather than scholarly renderings.
Alongside the diary are conquest letters (fetihname), the best known by the court historian Celalzade Mustafa, and later chronicles, tax registers and travellers. The European side has Jacques de Bourbon, Jacobus Fontanus, the later history by Bosio, and the Venetian diaries of Marino Sanuto. Where a familiar scene comes only from the European writers, I say so. Where the Ottoman sources say something different, I say that too.
A few notes. Piri Mehmed Pasha, the grand vizier, is a different man from Piri Reis the mapmaker, and the two are often confused. Ottoman and European calendars sat a day or two apart in places. Figures for troops, ships and dead are the least reliable thing on either side, and I treat them that way.

chapters.title: The sea road
chapters.text:
From Istanbul, Rhodes was not a picturesque fortress at the edge of the map. It was a cork in a bottle. Ships bound from Alexandria or the Syrian coast for the capital had to round the south-west corner of Anatolia, and Rhodes sat exactly there, with a harbour deep enough for galleys and a garrison that could be at sea within hours.
The Order of St John had held the island since the early fourteenth century. By the Ottoman reckoning, which Turkish historians still repeat, the Knights had made it a base for hostility: they joined alliances against the Ottomans, sheltered corsair ships, raided the Anatolian coast, and preyed on merchant and pilgrim shipping. The Knights saw the same activity as holy war in defence of Christendom. Both descriptions fit.
The Mediterranean was a sea where every power ran its own raiders, and the Ottomans had theirs. Kurtoğlu Muslihiddin Reis, who served in the 1522 fleet, was a corsair captain of exactly that kind. What set the Knights apart was that they were a state of their own, with a fortress, a treasury and a fleet, answerable to no sultan.
The human side of this was captivity. Muslim sailors, merchants and coastal villagers taken at sea ended up in Rhodes, rowing in the Order's galleys or labouring on the fortifications. Modern Turkish historians speak of thousands, and the Ottoman diary of 1522 pays attention to the prisoners in a way that suggests they mattered. I could not find a reliable count from either side. What can be said is that people on that coast knew someone who had been taken, and that Rhodes was where such people went.
In 1516 and 1517 the situation changed. Sultan Selim, Süleyman's father, conquered Syria and Egypt from the Mamluks. Almost overnight the Ottoman empire acquired Cairo, Jerusalem, Mecca and Medina, the grain and revenue of the Nile, and a new duty, the safe passage of pilgrims. The overland roads were long. The sea road from Istanbul to Alexandria was the natural one, and it ran past Rhodes. The Turkish encyclopaedia entry on the island puts it simply: after the conquest of Egypt, Rhodes sat on the most important sea route between the capital and the new provinces.
The Knights did not help their case. Turkish scholars cite their support for Canberdi Gazali, the former Mamluk governor of Damascus who rebelled against the Ottomans in Syria in 1520 and 1521, and complaints of attacks on Ottoman trade and pilgrim ships. I have not traced those complaints to individual incidents, so they are best read as the Ottoman case as later historians summarise it.
Selim himself, according to Turkish accounts, ordered a fleet prepared against Rhodes near the end of his reign, though he had earlier been cautious about the island because of Prince Cem, the subject of the next chapter. He died in September 1520 before it sailed. The decision passed, with the throne, to his son.

chapters.title: Unfinished business: Mesih Pasha and Prince Cem
chapters.text:
The Ottomans had tried Rhodes before. Naval raids in 1454 and 1455, in the early years of Mehmed II, did some damage on the eastern coast, and an expedition in 1467 achieved nothing. The serious attempt came in 1480, under Mesih Pasha.
Mesih Pasha is one of the odder figures of the age. He was born around 1443 into the Byzantine imperial family, the Palaiologoi, was taken as a boy when Constantinople fell, converted, and rose through the palace to become vizier and admiral. In May 1480 he landed on Rhodes and spent the summer pounding the Tower of St Nicholas and the south-east wall. European sources, led by the Order's own vice-chancellor Guillaume Caoursin, whose eyewitness account was in print within months, tell what happened next. On 27 July Ottoman troops broke into the town, were thrown out after hours of close fighting, and fled after seeing a golden cross and a woman in white in the sky.
Ottoman writers explain it differently. The later chronicler Hoca Sadeddin, as summarised by a modern Turkish historian, says the troops got in through the breaches and planted their flags, but that Mesih Pasha, who had at first promised plunder, changed his mind at the critical moment and declared that the treasury belonged to the sultan. The soldiers lost heart, no reinforcements went in behind the first wave, and the Knights recovered their ground. In this telling the siege was lost by a commander's broken promise, not by a miracle.
Mesih lost his vizierate and was sent to govern Gelibolu, though he returned to high office later. Hoca Sadeddin was writing a century afterwards, and I cannot say which account is closer to the events. But it matters that Ottoman tradition remembered 1480 as a lesson in managing an army.
The memory stayed in the vocabulary of the next siege. On 22 November 1522 the campaign diary records an assault on "the tower known as Mesih Pasha's Tower", in the sector of Piri Mehmed Pasha. Nobody on the Ottoman side in 1522 needed to be told who Mesih was.
The second wound was Prince Cem. After Mehmed's death in 1481, Cem fought his elder brother Bayezid for the throne and lost. In July 1482 he fled to Rhodes, and the Knights received him with ceremony. Within months the Grand Master, Pierre d'Aubusson, was also negotiating with Bayezid. By 1483 they had agreed that the Order would keep Cem under guard in return for an annual payment that sources put at 40,000 to 45,000 ducats. Cem was sent on to France, then Rome, and then toward Naples in the train of King Charles VIII, where he died in February 1495.
For the Ottomans this was a hostage business conducted in public. A son of the Conqueror, a man with a claim to the throne, was held in a Christian castle and used as a counter in European diplomacy, while the sultan paid his brother's keepers to keep him there. Every coalition that wished to threaten the dynasty knew where a pretender could be found. Turkish scholars argue that this made Bayezid cautious with the Knights, and that Selim hesitated over Rhodes for the same reason.
It did not end with Cem's death. His son Murad, according to Wikipedia's summary of European sources, ended up on Rhodes, took the Catholic name Pierre, and married into an Italian family. Turkish historians list the Knights' presentation of Murad as a possible claimant among the grievances that led to 1522. When Süleyman rode out several times that autumn to look at "the garden of Cem Sultan", as the diary records, the old business was still unsettled.

chapters.title: A young sultan's march
chapters.text:
Süleyman came to the throne in September 1520, in his mid-twenties, with no victories of his own. His father had doubled the empire in eight years. The young sultan needed to show that the dynasty's luck had passed to him intact.
He chose his first targets with care. In August 1521 his army took Belgrade, the great fortress on the Danube that Mehmed the Conqueror had failed to capture in 1456. Rhodes was the other place the Conqueror had not been able to take. Turkish historians say outright that part of the aim of 1522 was to wipe out the shame of the defeat of 1480. A sultan who took both within two years would not be mistaken for a boy.
Later narratives credit the grand vizier, Piri Mehmed Pasha, with urging the campaign and urging haste. He was an old servant of Selim's and had good reason to want the Egypt road secured. By September he was ill: the diary says his feet gave him trouble.
The fleet sailed first. According to Turkish scholarship it left Istanbul on 4 June 1522 under Mustafa Pasha, the second vizier, called Çoban Mustafa in most modern accounts and Balak or Pulak in some Turkish ones. The number of ships is disputed: Ottoman writers say 300 to 700, Western ones 250 to 400, and nobody can check either. The army figures run from 100,000 to 200,000.
Süleyman followed by land. On Monday 16 June he crossed to Üsküdar, and the diary begins counting marches: Maltepe, Hereke, İznik, Yenişehir. At Kütahya on 1 July the beylerbeyi of Anatolia, Kasım Pasha, the Janissary agha Balı Ağa and the agha of the azabs, Ali Bey, rode out to meet him with all their men, and there were festivities. The beylerbeyi of Rumelia arrived with his troops, divans were held, the lords of Anatolia brought gifts. An army on the road was a government in motion.
The news on the way was mixed. On 9 July a messenger from Mustafa Pasha, already at the coast, reported that there was no chance the castle would surrender by agreement. Couriers from Rumelia brought word of trouble on the Hungarian frontier, where the ban of Transylvania was moving against Wallachia, first on 24 June and again in November and December. The campaign ran with a clock ticking in the north.
On 24 July the diary records a small moment of impatience. A message from Ahmed Pasha, already at the shore, said the landing place was too crowded to cross. The sultan, the clerk writes, would not put up with it, and rode on toward the pier. On 26 July the household troops and Janissaries pressed to cross; the armies of Rumelia and Anatolia were already over. On 28 July Süleyman himself came across the strait. Every ship that was in the fleet fired its guns in salute, and from that day, the clerk says, they began to fight.
The fleet and advance forces had been on the island for weeks. European sources date the first landing to 26 June, near Ialysos. The Ottoman diary, and the modern editors who follow it, count the siege from the sultan's arrival, and date it to 29 July. Each side's calendar centres its own protagonist.
Before the siege, according to a Turkish summary of Ottoman sources, the sultan also sent a letter to the Grand Master setting out what would follow if the island surrendered, and got no answer. European chroniclers give their own versions of the exchange. I have not been able to verify either.

chapters.title: Columns, ditches and mines
chapters.text:
The Ottoman siege was not a single assault. It was a long engineering operation, and the diary shows it better than any other source I have read.
The first weeks were guns and earth. The army dug trenches and earthworks toward the walls, hauled its heavy guns forward, and fired mortars the diary calls "aerial guns", which dropped shot over the walls. By 1 August the clerk says the defenders were sounding a bell to warn of incoming fire and running underground. The Knights' gunnery was good, and the clerk knows it. On 30 August he records that every time the Ottoman gunners got a damaged piece working again, the defenders turned some thirty guns on it.
The men who ran the siege were the sultan's viziers and beylerbeyis, each with a column of his own. The diary names Mustafa Pasha, Ahmed Pasha, Piri Mehmed Pasha, Ayas Pasha and Kasım Pasha, and speaks also of an Anatolian column and a Rumelian one. Kasım Pasha was beylerbeyi of Anatolia, and Ayas Pasha, by late September, is called beylerbeyi of Rumelia. Ahmed Pasha appears more than any other at the breaches.
On 2 September he began battering "the prison tower", on 12 September he cut a hill in two to place guns beneath the wall, and on 19 September he began inspecting the lines in person. Modern English-language accounts call him an experienced siege engineer, and the diary does nothing to contradict that. Piri Mehmed Pasha's guns opened on 15 August. Kurtoğlu Muslihiddin Reis was given a squadron on 5 August with orders to attack from the sea on assault days.
I have not tried to match these columns to the Knights' posts, the langues of England, Spain, Provence and the rest. The diary does not use those names. The usual European account places the great mine of early September at the English post and the heaviest fighting at Spain. The Ottoman clerk simply speaks of breaches, towers and the outer wall, which he calls the hisar-ı beçe.
Reinforcements came from Egypt. On 9 August twenty-four ships under Hayır Bey, the former Mamluk emir who had gone over to Selim and governed Egypt for the Ottomans, ran in past the Knights' fire and joined the fleet without loss, the clerk says. Egyptian troops were given a place in the lines near Piri Mehmed Pasha's sector. On 20 September some Circassians in that sector went through a breach on their own initiative, took four or five banners and a board studded with nails, laid to cripple attackers' feet, and came back unhurt, saying they had gone in only to see whether there was a ditch behind. The diary does not say they were former Mamluks, but Circassians had been the backbone of the old regime in Cairo. Five years after the conquest of Egypt, men from that world were fighting on Rhodes under the Ottoman flag.
The fighting that mattered was underground, and the diary is candid about why. On 14 September it records that the Muslims understood that taking the fortress with cannon and musket was hard, perhaps impossible, so forty or fifty ghazis from Mustafa Pasha's column went down into the ditch with picks and crowbars and began to undermine the outer wall at its foot. Ahmed Pasha's column did the same. It is the nearest the diary comes to admitting that the original plan had not worked.
Mining came with the picks. The Ottoman sappers (lağımcı, a word that in modern Turkish means a sewer worker) packed galleries under the Knights' towers and fired them with powder, and the clerk logs the results. A mine in Mustafa Pasha's sector on 5 September brought down a tower and set off a general bombardment, so that the defenders thought an assault was coming; two more on 11 September let some men into the outer wall at heavy cost; a pair in Ahmed Pasha's on 18 September failed to open a way in. European accounts date the great mine under the English post to 4 September, one day earlier.
European narratives also tell of the Venetian engineer Gabriele Tadini, who listened for the sappers with a drum laid on the ground and blew up their galleries from below. The diary never names him. It does admit, on 16 September, that the defenders found and neutralised two of Kasım Pasha's mines, and it records on 22 September that when Mustafa Pasha's sappers heard the enemy digging toward them, the pasha said, "Light it now," and a number of defenders died. European writers name Bosnia and Wallachia as the homes of the miners. The Ottoman clerk does not say.
On 29 August the whole army was ordered to carry stones and timber to fill the ditch, and on 31 August, the diary says, the slaves and freedmen on the island, high and low, headed for the fortress to finish the job.

chapters.title: The twenty-fourth of September
chapters.text:
By the third week of September the clerk's entries change tone. On 15 September a council was held "on the matter of the conquest". On 18 September two mines in Ahmed Pasha's sector were fired and the men sitting behind the earthworks were meant to rush the breach, but no help came from the flanks, the debris fell back on them, and about 150 died. On 21 September the viziers and great lords gathered to prepare the assault, and Ahmed Pasha, Ayas Pasha and Balı Ağa were each given a robe of honour.
On 22 September a mine was lit in Mustafa Pasha's sector as the defenders were digging toward it. On 23 September a mine in Ahmed Pasha's sector did not work properly, and the attack was put off a day. From noon prayer until midnight criers went through every camp with the proclamation. In my translation: "Tomorrow at dawn the assault goes in from every side. The stones and earth belong to the Padishah; the other males and females, with their goods and property, are plunder for the ghazis."
That proclamation reads differently after 1480. Mesih Pasha, on the Ottoman tradition summarised earlier, promised plunder and then took it back. Süleyman's heralds did the opposite, and did it before the attack. The stones and earth of the town went to the sultan, which was the state's share.
Everything else was the soldiers'. In the usual understanding of Islamic law a city taken by storm could be sacked, whereas one that surrendered by agreement could not, so the heralds were setting the terms of the assault. What happened afterwards would depend on whether the defenders gave in first.
The attack came on Wednesday 24 September, before the dawn prayer. The clerk gives it a short paragraph. The assault went in from every side. There were three or four hours of fierce fighting.
The defenders threw fire-pots and incendiaries onto the Muslims as well as firing guns and muskets and hurling wood and stones. In the end the victorious troops, who saw that getting in was not possible, drew back, those who could. "Many people were martyred."
The diary says nothing of a Janissary standard on the Tower of Spain, or of the tower changing hands twice. That is the European picture, taken from the Knights' side: banners planted by noon, a tower lost and retaken. The Ottoman clerk writes only that entry was not possible. Both can be partly true, since a clerk writing for the sultan's archive need not record every flag. But the difference of emphasis is just what one would expect.
The aftermath is another place where the traditions part. In European accounts, Süleyman was furious with Mustafa Pasha, the commander of the assault, condemned him to death, and was talked out of it. The diary records on the next day only that slaves were sent into Anatolia to raise provisions for the camp. On 26 September it records a council at which the beylerbeyi of Rumelia, Ayas Pasha, "fell into disgrace and was imprisoned, because on the day of the assault he marched later than the others". The next day, at another council, he was released and his post confirmed. On 28 September he was sent with the whole Rumelian army to take over Piri Mehmed Pasha's sector, since Piri's feet were troubling him.
So the Ottoman diary has a punished commander, and the European accounts have a punished commander, but they are not the same man. The Knights could only have learned what was said in the sultan's tent from prisoners and deserters, so the story of Mustafa's sentence may be a garbled version of Ayas's arrest, or the clerk may have left one out. What the diary says of Mustafa Pasha comes a month later. On 25 October he was told to go to Egypt to guard it, and on 28 October he left with fifteen ships. News of the death of Hayır Bey, the governor of Egypt, had arrived two days before the order. That looks more like a transfer to a province that suddenly needed a governor than a punishment, though the clerk gives no reason.
On 29 September a gunner from the Morea walked out of the fortress, surrendered and became a Muslim. He told the Ottomans that the defenders had lost one of their lords killed, another wounded and about three hundred men, and was given a robe. The same day, fifteen sailors who had secretly ferried some soldiers "to the other shore" were hanged from the yardarms; the clerk does not say which shore, and deserters are the obvious reading. On 30 September news came that a son had been born to the sultan, and the imperial drums were beaten in celebration, in the middle of the siege.
In the European story 24 September is the day the Order's survival began to look like a miracle. In the Ottoman story it is the day an army learned how much work was left.

chapters.title: The people of the army
chapters.text:
The diary is written about the sultan and his viziers, but the army shows through it. It was a large and mixed body of men, and few of them were professional soldiers in the modern sense.
At the centre were the Janissaries, the sultan's own infantry, recruited as boys and paid from the treasury. Their agha, Balı Ağa, was wounded in the assault of 12 October and appears again at the surrender, leading 150 men into the town. Alongside them were the gunners, respected for their skill and exposed to counterfire. The diary records the death on 26 August of a gunner called Mehmed, the master gunner's son, "known for his skill in his craft", and on 12 September it records that the master gunner's own foot was injured by a shot and that he died the next day.
The provincial cavalry, the sipahis of Anatolia and Rumelia, appear in the diary mostly when they die: on 18 August a ditch wall collapsed and buried "a good many" of them. The azabs were light infantry raised for a campaign and sent home afterwards, and the diary shows their agha, Ali Bey, riding out to meet the sultan at Kütahya with all of them. Beyond these were household troops, volunteers, craftsmen and camp followers. On 24 November the army was told to enrol five hundred volunteers (gönüllü), and on 27 November they were given a captain.
A siege on this scale called for trades. On 12 September the army's artisans, "the people of the companies and the other craftsmen", were ordered to Ahmed Pasha's lines to help with the ditch. On 6 December armour was issued to the troops in Piri Mehmed Pasha's sector. Supplies came by ship and by levy: on 25 September slaves were sent to Anatolia to raise provisions, and on 13 November two ships brought gunpowder from Istanbul.
The ordinary soldier's experience was mostly digging, waiting and rain. On 18 November a gale rose at nightfall and wrecked seven ships, with many drowned. On 22 November, the day of a failed assault, a state galley was dashed on the rocks and all its people drowned. On 9 December the rain fell "beyond measure" and torrents ran through the lines.
Casualties were heavy, though the diary gives no total. It counts in tens and hundreds: about 150 killed on 18 September in the failed mine, 50 or 60 on 11 October going into and out of the ditch, 40 or 50 on 22 November, six on 14 November from a single shot. European writers and some modern summaries give figures from 50,000 to over 100,000, but they are round numbers of the kind both sides produced, and I have not found an Ottoman total to set against them. The clerk calls the dead martyrs (şehit).
Voices come through now and then. On 13 September, the diary says, some Muslims at the head of the earthworks called out to the defenders that they were suffering in vain and should surrender, since the army would not leave without the fortress, and the defenders called back that the Muslims were the ones suffering in vain and would never take it. On 11 October, when guns picked off men going in and out of the ditch, the clerk says the people of Islam "paid no heed to their guns and muskets and went on digging down the wall with heart and soul". On 27 August the diary relays a deserter's report that the Knights' own gunners had boasted that no man would walk the island, and had answered their Grand Master's rebuke with the words, "We did not know the Turk would come from under the earth."
The captives are the most striking subject of the last week. On 23 December officials were sent into the fortress to inspect the prisoners and free them from chains and dungeons. On 24 December most of the captives came out, and the camps were full of them. On 28 December the sultan gave money in alms to the prisoners. The diary does not say how many there were or how many were Muslims, but the modern Turkish editors of the diary list the freeing of thousands of Muslims held on Rhodes among the aims of the campaign.
Then there was plunder. The cry of 23 September had made it the soldiers' reward, and the terms of surrender, as the next chapters show, took it away. The ranks had spent months digging and bleeding in the rain for a surrender that gave them the sultan's thanks. The diary records that robes and gifts were given to the great men and that winter clothing was issued to the lords. What the ordinary soldiers thought is not recorded.

chapters.title: Winter coming
chapters.text:
October brought the first real doubts about the calendar. On 3 October the clerk notes, with some understatement, that there were "many signs of winter" and that the ships were preparing to go to another harbour. The fleet could not stay on an open coast through the autumn gales, and an army without a fleet could not be supplied.
The outer wall, the hisar-ı beçe, went in stages. On 7 October about two thousand Muslims surged forward at the hour of the afternoon prayer, shouting the call to prayer and the takbir, and planted a flag on the outer work and took one of the towers attached to it. On 15 October a breach was taken in the evening and the defenders left the barbican empty. On 17 October the rest of it fell in a night attack.
The sultan's own days appear in small pieces. He rode out to see the siege lines, and rode out to the old fortress the diary calls "Old Rhodes", which he ordered rebuilt from the foundations on 13 October and which the diary reports finished on 19 December. It is usually taken to be the old hill-fortress at Ialysos, though I have not verified that. On 16 October, and again on 20 November, 19 December and 22 December, the diary says he rode to look at the garden of Cem Sultan. We do not know what the garden was, but the obvious reading is an orchard associated with the prince's stay forty years earlier. It is the one place in the diary where the unfinished business of Cem is allowed to show.
News from outside kept arriving. On 23 October a boat from Egypt brought word of the death of Hayır Bey, the governor. On 25 October Mustafa Pasha was sent to Egypt. On 1 November the viziers began making plans for wintering, and on 8 November the fleet went off to the harbour at Marmaris, though it was recalled for the assaults at the end of the month.
On 3 December Mustafa's courier reported Egypt calm. From the north came word on 15 November that the ban of Transylvania had resumed operations in Wallachia, and on 16 December that the King of Hungary meant to march "as soon as the Danube freezes". The frontier lords were ordered to gather. An absent sultan was an invitation, and every week on Rhodes made it more likely.
The rain came in November. On 12 and 22 November assaults on towers in Ahmed Pasha's and Piri Mehmed Pasha's sectors failed. The tower of Mesih Pasha fell on 26 November at a second attempt. On 29 November a "great battle" was fought from Ahmed Pasha's breach, with the fleet joining in from the sea, in heavy rain; many died and the attack failed. The next day the army set about digging into the four inner ditches behind the wall. On 20 November a heavy bombardment had ruined, the clerk says, about half the area of the town.
Then something shifted. On 1 December a deserter reported that the defenders had lost over three hundred in the last attack and were badly weakened; an assault ordered for the next morning was cancelled. On 4 December the trench of Kasım Pasha reached the houses inside the fortress. On 9 December, in a flood of rain, Ahmed Pasha's trenches reached the middle of the town and forty or fifty houses were taken. It was not an assault. It was a siege tightening.
On 10 December the defenders asked for terms. The Ottomans agreed to a truce and sent in two men, the master of the hounds and the steward of Ahmed Pasha. On 13 December a deserter said the offer was a trick: the defenders had heard that relief was coming and wanted to gain time. On 14 December fighting resumed.
Overnight, about 150 men arrived by ship from outside. On 16 December the Ottoman admiral, Balak Mustafa Bey, was dismissed and the post given to Behram Bey, the lord of Avlonya. The clerk gives the cause as "yesterday's matter", presumably the ships that had run in.
On the same day the diary records, without comment, that two Christians captured from the defenders were sent back inside with their hands, arms and noses cut off. Neither side should be spared the cruelty the siege produced. European narratives report that the Order hanged and quartered a servant, Blas Diez, on 6 November and beheaded the Portuguese chancellor Andrea d'Amaral for treason soon after. The Ottoman diary reports, also on 6 November, that one of the castle's lords who wanted to submit was quartered by the others, with a piece hung up at each breach. The date matches the European date for Diez's execution, so the two may be one story told from opposite sides. I would not press the identification.

chapters.title: The surrender and its terms
chapters.text:
The talks of 10 to 14 December had failed, but the pressure behind them had not gone. On 17 December the Grand Master sent word that he would give the sultan his word, but that a party of hard-liners would not agree. A deserter said the Knights could not agree among themselves. On 18 December another section of the outer wall fell.
On 19 December, the diary says, the defenders came out and submitted. They asked for ten days, and the Grand Master named fifty-three men, headed by the lord of Kos, as hostages. At midnight they came out, the ten days began, and five hundred of the sultan's household cavalry were set to watch them.
On 20 December three leading townsmen came to the divan and said that until now they had been the ones who refused, but that they were now entirely the sultan's subjects. Written guarantees (ahidname) were issued to them, and each was given a robe. The clerk dates the surrender to the first of the month of Safer, which Turkish sources put at 20 or 21 December. European narratives usually say 22 December.
What were the terms? The diary does not list them. A Turkish historian summarising later narratives, which go back in part to the nineteenth-century Austrian historian Hammer, gives them thus. The Knights had ten days to leave Rhodes and the other islands, taking what they could carry. All prisoners, Muslim and Christian, held on Rhodes were to be returned to the Turks. Four thousand Janissaries under their agha were to occupy the harbour and watch the embarkation, and the army was to keep a mile from the fortress.
Twenty-five senior Knights and twenty-five leading townsmen were to be held as hostages. Anyone from the town could go with the Knights. After the Turks entered there was to be no plunder and nobody was to be taken captive. The islanders were to pay no tax for five years. Catholics were to have the same freedom as the Orthodox.
European summaries agree on most of this and add three points. They say the Knights had twelve days, not ten. They say the islanders had three years to leave if they wished. And they say churches were not to be desecrated or turned into mosques.
I cannot confirm the last clause in the Ottoman material I have read. Some modern summaries add an exemption from the boy-levy for the Janissaries (the devshirme), but I found no reliable source for it and would not repeat it. The hostage numbers also differ: fifty in the Turkish summary and fifty-three in the diary.
These were generous terms by the standards of the day, and it helps to see why. On 23 September the heralds had announced that the town's people were plunder. By 19 December the Ottomans had every reason to prefer agreement: winter was closing in, Hungary was stirring, and the army was worn out. That does not make the terms less real. The Knights left, and the townspeople were, at least on paper, protected.
Not everyone trusted this. On 22 December four townsmen came to the camp to complain that the Knights wanted to conscript them to row the galleys. The clerk gives no outcome. On 23 December the Ottomans sent thirty caulkers in to help repair the ships for the departure.
On 24 December troops from the columns of Piri Mehmed Pasha and Ahmed Pasha entered the fortress, with Balı Ağa and 150 Janissaries. At noon on 25 December, the diary says, the sultan's muezzins gave the call to prayer from a tower the clerk calls the Tower of the Arab, the red-and-yellow banner of the Janissaries was raised there, the imperial drums beat, and the cry of "Allah, Allah" went up from every corner of the fortress. The sultan himself is not recorded as entering the town that day. He rode out to look at Old Rhodes, gave money on the road to three townspeople walking to their villages, and let the hostages go back in.
A tradition told in European books says Süleyman rode in on Christmas Day through the Gate of St Athanasios, as far as the church of St John, and had the gate sealed afterwards. Porter, writing in 1858, cites a Turkish source for the Christmas visit. The Ottoman diary has no such scene, and its first record of the sultan touring the fortress is on 29 December.
The meeting with the Grand Master is the best-known scene of the surrender, and the two traditions tell it differently. In the diary, on Friday 26 December, "Megali Mastori", as the Ottomans rendered the title, came to the imperial divan with the lords under him and kissed the sultan's hand. He brought gifts of bowls, dishes and cups, which the clerk lists. He came again on 1 January, kissed the hand a second time, and presented four ingots of gold, each said to be worth a thousand florins. At midnight he and his followers boarded boats and sailed out, taking the great ship with them.
The European tradition, from Bosio and the writers on whom he drew, tells a longer story: a sultan impressed by the old man's dignity, an offer of rank for conversion that Villiers refused, and Süleyman remarking that it was not without compunction that he forced so venerable a soldier to seek a new home. I have not been able to trace that remark to a contemporary text. It is the sort of thing a defeated Order would want to remember, and it may also be true.
On 27 December the diary records the hardest scene of the surrender, in a single flat entry. "The late Cem Sultan's son, a man of middle age, was found in the dress of the infidels, and he was killed. It was said he had a son and daughters; the son was also killed, and the daughters and the woman were ordered sent to Istanbul." The prince is not named. European and Wikipedia accounts call him Murad and say two of his sons died; some historians question whether the victims can be identified so exactly. The diary has one son killed. However many, the business of Cem was settled in this way.
The terms did not last long. On Friday 2 January 1523, hours after the Knights sailed, the diary says the Friday prayer was held in the church the Ottomans called Sencovan, which is San Giovanni, the Order's conventual church. The mufti, Şeyh Ali, led the prayer and preached. After the prayer the sultan boarded the galley of the late sea captain Kara Mahmud and sailed for Marmaris.
A modern study of Ottoman buildings in Rhodes, citing earlier Turkish work, gives 20 January 1523 for the first Friday prayer in the church as the Great Mosque, the Cami-i Kebir. The two dates may mark different occasions, but I cannot tell. If the terms did include a promise about churches, it was broken within two weeks, in the church that mattered most.
On 11 January, riding home through Anatolia, he stopped to hunt cranes and ducks on the plain of Çine. On 29 January 1523 he rode back into Istanbul, 233 days after he had left.

chapters.title: A Muslim town in a Frankish shell
chapters.text:
Rhodes, after the Knights, was a fortress that needed a garrison, a town that needed people, and an island that needed a government. The Ottomans took them in that order.
The garrison came first. On 30 December the sultan assigned 500 castle guards and 500 Janissaries to hold the fortress, and by the 1530s the tax registers count 1,378 soldiers inside. On 4 January the diary names four sanjak beys, from Menteşe, Karasi, Aydın and Saruhan, who were to repair the walls with the men of their districts, and two days later Anatolian troops under four more beys crossed for the same work. Rhodes was too new to be a sanjak of its own, so for the moment it was attached to Mytilene.
A Turkish scholar writes that the island was first entrusted to Kurtoğlu Muslihiddin Reis, the corsair captain of the 1522 fleet. It later became a sanjak in the province of the Kapudan Pasha, the admiral of the fleet, and its sanjak bey was given four galleys and five boats. Repairs went on for years, and were still under way in 1525.
The town was the harder problem. About 4,000 Rhodians left with the Knights. The tax registers of the 1530s record 864 taxpaying households in the town: 591 Muslim, 144 Jewish and 129 Christian. Many of the Muslims were settlers. The Ottoman state used settlement as a tool of conquest, and a Turkish study says Süleyman gave land to Turks who came to Rhodes and freed them from tax and military service.
The Jewish households have a tradition attached. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 says Süleyman moved about 150 families from Salonica to Rhodes in 1523, with twenty years of tax freedom and a house each. It is reported as tradition, and I have not seen the firman. The registers find 144 Jewish households a few years later, which is a plausible match.
The Jewish quarter lay in the east of the walled town. Its community built Kahal Shalom in 1577, ran its own rabbinical court, and by about 1900 the Jewish Encyclopedia could say that the commerce of the island was largely in Jewish hands. In 1840, when the Jews were accused of ritual murder after a Greek boy went missing and a provincial governor tortured them, an imperial commission acquitted them, dismissed the governor, and the sultan's firman called the charge pure calumny.
The Christians were pushed outwards. A Turkish architectural historian, summarising Ottoman sources, writes that most non-Muslims were settled in the suburbs, the varoş, "for security reasons", while inside the walls only the garrison, the Muslim civilians and a few Christian families of special status could live. The Turkish encyclopaedia puts the number of such households at 45. The Greeks called the suburbs the marasia. Over the centuries this became a rule, and it is the best-known feature of Ottoman Rhodes.
The Oxford scholar Henry Tozer, who came ashore in April 1886, found it in force: "The gates of the city are closed at night, and no Christians are allowed to remain within the walls," he wrote, so the Greeks who kept shops there had to leave at sunset. He added that until some decades before there had been a further rule that all Christians must leave before noon on Fridays, in case the town were retaken while the faithful were at prayer. A report on the Muslim community repeats a tradition that Christians caught inside after dark could be beheaded. I have found no primary source for that.
The Ottomans did not close the island's churches, and Orthodox worship continued. Under the Knights the Greek clergy had answered to a Latin archbishop; that hierarchy left with the Order, and the Orthodox Metropolitan, seated in the suburbs, was again the Greeks' own judge and teacher. A Turkish article describes the Orthodox as left free to worship with their churches and monasteries untouched. Greek accounts stress the restrictions: new churches in the suburbs appear only after permission was given in the mid-eighteenth century.
The buildings changed hands too. The conventual church of St John became the great mosque, the Cami-i Kebir, and stayed one until 1856, when lightning struck the gunpowder stored beneath it. Churches across the town became small mosques, often with a minaret and mihrab added, and gave their names to neighbourhoods: Ilk Mihrab, "first prayer-niche", for the church of Agia Aikaterini; Dolaplı, "with cupboards", for Agia Triada. The Turkish encyclopaedia counts sixteen mosques and two Friday mosques in the walls by 1524, and the census of 1831 lists twenty-three Muslim neighbourhoods and two Jewish ones.
The sultan's own foundation was the largest. Süleyman endowed a vakıf of mosque, medrese, soup kitchen and bath, funded by the revenues of Rhodes and Kos. The Süleymaniye mosque is traditionally the first mosque of the conquest, raised in 1522 or 1523 on a church site. A study of Rhodes's Ottoman architecture says Ottoman sources date it to an order of 1541, and the building one sees is a rebuilding of 1808.
The Ibrahim Pasha mosque, dated by inscription to 1540 or 1541, is the oldest on the island and the only one regularly used for prayer today; tradition ties it to Süleyman's grand vizier Pargalı Ibrahim, passing through on the way to Egypt, which sits awkwardly with the inscribed date. Later centuries added the Rejep Pasha mosque (1588), the Murad Reis mosque (about 1623), the Mustafa Pasha mosque (about 1765) with the Yeni Hamam beside it, and the library of Hafiz Ahmed Agha (1793), whose founder, a chief equerry of the sultan born in a village south of the town, endowed it "for the literate public of his hometown" by a deed made in Istanbul in 1792. His descendants still run the foundation.
Rhodes had two other roles. It was a place of exile. The Crimean khan Canibek Giray, deposed in the 1630s, died on the island, and his tomb stands in the Murad Reis cemetery. The cemetery's namesake, the corsair-admiral Murad Reis, is hard to pin down: the dates and careers given for him in modern sources do not agree.
And it was a naval station. In 1748 enslaved Hungarians, Georgians and Maltese aboard a ship called the Lupa rose against their captors and sailed to Malta with over 150 Ottoman prisoners, including the former pasha of Rhodes. The old war at sea between the Order and the sultans had not ended in 1522. The Knights reached Malta in 1530, and in 1565 the sultan's fleets besieged them there.
By the late nineteenth century the sunset rule hides a changed town. The Ottoman provincial yearbook of 1903 counted 1,072 Muslim and 295 Jewish households inside the walls and 938 households in the suburbs. Cretan Muslim refugees of 1897 were settled outside the fortress. Tozer wrote that in 1886 the Ottoman sentries would not let a visitor stop to look at the walls or to sketch them.

chapters.title: What a visitor can still see
chapters.text:
Rhodes stopped being Ottoman in May 1912, when Italy occupied it during the war with the Ottoman Empire. It was Italian until 1943, then German, then British, and joined Greece in 1947 and 1948. For most of that century the island's story has been told as the story of the Knights, with the Ottomans as the interval between the walls and the present.
The Italians made choices. A summary on the city's Wikipedia page says they preserved what was left from the Knights' period and destroyed the Ottoman buildings. That is too neat, since much Ottoman fabric survives, but it points the right way. The Italians cut the Gate of Liberty through the walls in 1924 and presented themselves, according to Wikipedia's article on the fortifications, as liberators from Ottoman rule.
The island's Muslims were not moved. Because Rhodes was Italian in 1923, they were not part of the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, and when it joined Greece they became Greek citizens. Estimates of their number today range from about 2,000 to about 4,000. Many descend from Anatolian settlers of the sixteenth century onward, or from Cretan Muslims who came after 1897.
Many left for Turkey, especially after 1967 and 1974, and the Turkish-language schools were closed in 1972. The mosques, cemeteries and other pious property are managed by a state-supervised foundation, the Vakouf of Rhodes. A Council of Europe rapporteur found the community generally well integrated, with about a third regularly attending mosque, mostly older people. An anthropologist who has worked with it reports that for decades official guides were told not to mention the Ottoman past, and that this is now changing.
In Turkey the conquest is remembered as one of Süleyman's great early victories. Turkish scholarship on it is substantial: the campaign diary has been transcribed twice, in 2004 and 2017, there are studies of the fetihnames, and a survey of Turkish monuments in Rhodes was published by the Turkish Historical Society in 1986. I have not surveyed popular memory, so I would not generalise about how ordinary people see it. Ferries link Marmaris and Rhodes in the season, and the crossing the sultan made in July 1522 is a short one.
The Old Town offers a few things for someone who wants to see the other shore.
The Roloi clock tower in its present form is Ottoman, credited to Ahmed Fethi Pasha, who endowed a timekeeper's house and a school beside it in the early 1850s. Beside it stands the Süleymaniye, rose-pink, built on the site of a church, rebuilt in 1808, and mostly closed. Reports of its opening hours conflict. Across the lane is the Hafiz Ahmed Agha library, whose hours are posted on the door; a recent visitor found it locked.
The Gate of St Athanasios, tradition says, is where Süleyman entered on Christmas Day, before ordering it walled up. That tradition comes from European sources, and the Ottoman diary does not mention it. The Tower of Spain and the Terreplein of England along the moat are where European accounts place the great mine of early September and the hardest fighting of 24 September. The diary does not name these posts, so I would not claim to point to the spot where the Ottoman miners worked. But the moat they dug through is the moat one walks, and the moat is generally open and free.
On the east side, Agia Aikaterini is called Ilk Mihrab because tradition says Süleyman prayed there first. The Ottoman diary records the call to prayer from a tower on Christmas Day and the Friday prayer in the Sencovan church on 2 January. It says nothing of Agia Aikaterini, so the Ilk Mihrab story is a later local tradition that I cannot check against the Ottoman record.
The Ibrahim Pasha mosque on Platonos Square is a working mosque and should be approached as one. The Rejep Pasha mosque on Dorieos Square has been closed because of damage, and a study of Rhodes's Ottoman architecture reports that the Dutch historian Machiel Kiel recorded its tiles as deliberately smashed in 1976. The Mustafa Pasha mosque, used as a wedding office by the Muslim community, and the Yeni Hamam stand on Arionos Square; the bath is reported variously as restored and as closed. Greek press reports describe restoration work at several of these places in 2025 and 2026, and I have not checked which are open.
The cemetery behind the Mandraki waterfront, at the Murad Reis mosque, is the quietest of the Ottoman sites. Turbaned gravestones stand under eucalyptus trees, with the tomb of the exiled Crimean khan among them, a place to think of Rhodes as somewhere the empire sent its unwanted people. Lawrence Durrell lived in the gatekeeper's lodge in 1945. It has been neglected and often closed, and is worth checking before going.
One last timing is worth noting. The diary's Friday prayer in the church of St John falls on the day Süleyman left. The Knights had sailed that night, the pretender's son was dead, the soldiers were going home without plunder, and the Danube frontier was waiting. He was in Istanbul on 29 January. Ottoman Rhodes then lasted until 1912, about 390 years, and what a visitor sees of it is a town that was made from the Knights' own stones into something else.

sources:
A note on the evidence

The familiar story of 1522 comes mostly from the Order's side: Hospitaller writers and the Italian, French and German chroniclers who wrote from their reports. The Ottoman side offers something different in kind, a campaign diary kept day by day by clerks of the sultan's household, which records engineering, orders and casualties in small flat entries and says little about heroism. Neither side is neutral. Ottoman court writers wrote for a dynasty and presented conquest as divine favour. European writers wrote to raise funds and to explain a defeat as a kind of victory.

Some famous scenes rest on the European side alone: the Christmas Day entry through the Gate of St Athanasios, the sultan's remark about the old Grand Master, the sentence on Mustafa Pasha, the golden cross seen over the walls in 1480. The Ottoman diary has none of them, though absence from a clerk's notes is not proof that a thing did not happen. Some Ottoman claims rest on later chroniclers, such as the explanation of 1480 attributed to Hoca Sadeddin. Figures for armies, fleets and the dead are unreliable on both sides. The names Kemalpaşazade, Piri Reis and Matrakçı Nasuh are sometimes attached to the Rhodes story; I could not verify anything specific about 1522 in their works and I do not rely on them for any claim above.

The campaign diary is quoted in the author's own paraphrase translation from the printed Turkish transcription. Dates in it follow an Ottoman calendar that does not always match modern conversion tables by a day.

Ottoman primary sources

  • Rhodes campaign diary (ruzname), preserved in Feridun Bey, Münşeatü's-Selâtîn (compiled 1570s). Transcribed in Mehmet Yaşar Ertaş and Hacer Kılıçaslan, "Rodos'un Fetih Günlüğü: Kanuni Sultan Süleyman'ın Rodos Seferi Rûznâmesi", Akademik İncelemeler Dergisi 12/1 (2017), pp. 1-36 (PDF). The main Ottoman source for this piece: dates, commanders, mining, assaults, negotiations, the entry, the Friday prayer, the death of Cem's son. An earlier, incomplete edition is M. Akif Erdoğru, Tarih İncelemeleri Dergisi 19/1 (2004).
  • Celalzade Mustafa Çelebi, Rhodes fetihname, and the fetihname of the poet Fehmi. Known to me only through modern articles about them; I did not read the texts, and nothing above depends on them.
  • Hoca Sadeddin, Tacü't-Tevarih (late 16th century), cited through Cabir Doğan for the account of Mesih Pasha's reversal on plunder in 1480.
  • Evliya Çelebi, Seyahatname (visit to Rhodes, 1671), cited through the modern studies below.
  • Ottoman tax registers (tahrir) and provincial yearbooks (salname), for the household counts of the 1530s and 1903, cited through Doğan.

European primary sources

  • Guillaume Caoursin, Obsidionis Rhodiae urbis descriptio (1480). The Order's own eyewitness account of 1480, including the apparition story.
  • Jacques de Bourbon (1525), Jacobus Fontanus, De bello Rhodio, and Giacomo Bosio's later history of the Order. The main European narratives of 1522. I relied on them only through modern summaries.
  • Whitworth Porter, A History of the Knights of Malta (1858). A 19th-century narrative that preserves the Christmas Day entry and the Grand Master's audience as the European tradition tells them.
  • H. F. Tozer, The Islands of the Aegean (1890). A first-hand description of Ottoman Rhodes in April 1886, including the sunset rule for Christians.

Modern scholarship

  • Cabir Doğan, "Fethinden Kaybına Rodos (1522-1912)", SDÜ Fen Edebiyat Fakültesi Sosyal Bilimler Dergisi 30 (2013), pp. 67-88 (PDF). Ottoman motives, the Turkish summary of the surrender terms, administration, population figures.
  • "Rodos", TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi (online). Strategic reasons, the Süleyman endowment, the garrison and the early population.
  • Eric Brockman, The Two Sieges of Rhodes, 1480-1522 (1969). The standard English-language narrative, cited by the encyclopaedia entry above; used here only at second hand.
  • Zeki Çelikkol, Rodos'taki Türk Eserleri ve Tarihçe (Türk Tarih Kurumu, 1986), and Evliyaoğlu, Art-Sanat 17 (2022) on Ottoman buildings in Rhodes. Used at second hand for mosque dates and the first Friday prayer in the church of St John.
  • Wikipedia, "Siege of Rhodes (1522)", "Cem Sultan", "Şehzade Murad (son of Cem Sultan)" and "Sanjak of Rhodes". Used for the European outline, Cem's biography and the later administration. Handle with the usual care.
  • The Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), "Rhodes". Source for the traditions about the 1523 resettlement of Salonican Jews and the 1840 blood libel.
  • Human Rights Without Frontiers, report on the Muslim minority of Rhodes (2015); a Council of Europe rapporteur's report on the Muslim minority in Greece; and the anthropologist Kira Kaurinkoski's conference abstract (2011). Used for the present-day community. The HRWF report is an advocacy source.
